How Are U.S. Recruiting Agencies Surviving a Tougher Job Market?

The recruitment industry is facing a difficult equation: millions of job seekers, cautious employers, intense competition for openings, and growing pressure to control operating costs.

Yet recruiting agencies are adapting.

Some of these agencies have been forced to reduce their dependence on expensive physical offices and embracing remote or hybrid operations.

Others are investing in AI, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and virtual interviews to manage larger candidate pools more efficiently.

Many are strengthening relationships with employers by offering flexible staffing, specialized recruitment and workforce solutions.

The market is challenging, but it is not disappearing. The U.S. had 7.3 million job openings in July 2026, while temporary and contract staffing employment was 5.5% higher year-over-year in August, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and American Staffing Association.

The bigger question is:

Are recruitment agencies becoming more efficient, or are they simply being forced to reinvent themselves?

Perhaps the future of recruiting will be leaner, more digital, more specialized and increasingly remote.

"Hiring an Order-to-Cash Contractor? Here's What Sets the Right One Apart."

Order-to-Cash Isn't Just Billing and Collections. It's the Entire Revenue Lifecycle — and Most Contractors Only Know Pieces of It. 🌐

If you're hiring OTC support for a global operation, you're not just looking for someone who can send invoices and chase payments. You need someone who understands the full lifecycle — order entry, contract terms, billing, cash application, collections, credit risk, and reconciliation — as one connected system, not five separate tasks handed to five different people.

Here's what actually separates a capable OTC contractor from the right one:

🌍 Global fluency, not just remote availability. Multi-currency invoicing, cross-border payment timing, and regional compliance quirks aren't edge cases in international OTC — they're Tuesday. I've worked international financial services for 15+ years, remote and global, specifically inside this complexity.

🔍 A fraud examiner's read on "normal." As a Certified Fraud Examiner (ACFE) and ex-Fraud Analyst at JPMorgan Chase, I don't just process the full order-to-cash cycle — I know what a manipulated discount, a suspicious write-off, or a manufactured dispute looks like at every stage of it.

🤖 AI-assisted execution, human-supervised. I run OTC workflows daily inside Claude and Gemini-assisted systems — fast where automation should be fast, and with a human checkpoint exactly where judgment can't be delegated.

🔄 Full-cycle ownership, not task-based execution. I don't just "do billing" or "do collections." I manage the full order-to-cash system end to end, which means I catch the problems that only show up when you can see how one stage affects the next.

Most companies hiring OTC support end up with someone who's good at one segment of the cycle and blind to how it connects to the rest. That gap is exactly where cash gets stuck and fraud gets missed.

 ✅ Ex-Fraud Analyst, JPMorgan Chase
 ✅ 15+ years international financial services — remote, global, full-cycle OTC
 ✅ Claude & Gemini AI User

A local entity does not solve the compliance coordination problem.

A local company can unlock contracts, hiring, invoicing, tax registration, and certain operating steps.

It cannot decide how product, data, payments, customer acquisition, and partner activity fit together.

That coordination is where market-entry risk usually lives.

A fintech team may have an entity and still need answers on the customer journey, payment partners, data access, sales claims, customer support, and which activities require a licensed local counterparty.

An AI provider may employ a local team and still need evidence on data handling, deployment, model governance, and accountability when a system fails.

The operating requirement is a single cross-functional map. For each customer-facing route, show:

• The activity.
• The responsible owner.
• The relevant adviser or counterparty.
• The approval needed.
• The consequence of delay.

Entity setup is a foundation. Coordination is the work that allows the foundation to carry weight.

The key shift is from reactive hiring to proactive capability planning:

Forecast the capability → Build the pipeline → Develop internal talent → Access specialized expertise → Deploy when needed.

At 360 IDE, we believe successful IT staffing goes beyond filling today’s vacancies. It’s about helping organizations prepare for the technology capabilities they will need next—through W2, contract, contract-to-hire, and permanent talent solutions.

Strategy creates future demand. Capability readiness determines whether you can meet it.

Legal firms are about to lose their next generation of partners and most haven't noticed yet.

Here's the problem nobody's saying out loud.

The training ground for partners was the work. Years of grinding through documents, contracts, briefs. That work built the judgment. AI is doing most of it now.

So where exactly does the next partner come from?

The pipeline was built on a foundation that's quietly disappearing.

And if analytical horsepower is no longer the thing you hire for, what fills that gap?

My instinct says trust. AI cannot sit across from someone in a difficult legal matter, look them in the eye, and say it's on their side. A person can. That relationship might end up being the whole job, and right now almost nobody is hiring or training for it.

That's the question I work through with firms. Not handing them an answer. Sitting down and figuring out what a great lawyer looks like at their firm, specifically. Then building that into how they develop people.

So their succession plan is one their competitors aren't even thinking about yet.

And the board can say something real: we are changing the skills our people will need. Before it becomes urgent.

Law is just one example. Every professional services firm is staring at the same problem, whether they've named it or not.

A telecom infrastructure company had bought three AI recruiting tools in eighteen months. None of them were in daily use.

That's the pattern we see most. The demos were good. The pilots ran on a handful of reqs. Then the tool sat next to the ATS, recruiters kept working the old way, and the license renewed anyway.

They brought us in to sort it out. Not to pick a fourth tool.

We started by mapping where recruiter hours actually went across [40] open reqs, from field technician roles to RF engineering. 
Scheduling and hiring manager follow-up ate [35] percent of the week. Sourcing, which was where two of the three tools pointed, was under [15].

Then we ran the three tools they already owned against that map. One did a job nobody needed. One overlapped with a feature already inside their ATS. One was good, badly configured, and switched off by default for half the team.

We killed two contracts, reconfigured the third, and added one scheduling and interview-intelligence layer where the hours were going. Every recruiter got two hours of training built around their own reqs, not a vendor deck. 

Adoption was tracked weekly for the first [8] weeks, and anyone not using the tools got a call from their manager, not from us.

The recruiting team is the same size it was. It just stopped doing scheduling.

AI in TA fails at the rollout, not the purchase. Fix the rollout.

A Fortune 1000 manufacturer came to us with a familiar problem: hiring that arrived in waves. A new plant line, a contract win, a product launch, and suddenly [120] open roles landed on a team built for [30]. 

The pattern each time was the same. Agencies got called in at [25 percent] fees, time-to-fill stretched past [70] days, and the in-house recruiters spent the surge doing scheduling instead of recruiting.

We did three things over [14] weeks.
-First, we built a surge model. We mapped the last two years of req volume against the business calendar and found the spikes were predictable [8 to 10] weeks out. That gave the team a trigger point instead of a fire drill.
-Second, we placed [6] Beacon recruiters and sourcers inside the team for the next spike, working in the client's ATS under the client's process, so hiring managers saw one team, not a vendor.
-Third, we put AI in the middle of the process. Scheduling ran itself, interview notes were summarized before debriefs, and stalled reqs got flagged on day five.

The results from the first surge: [110] hires in [9] weeks, agency spend down [X percent], time-to-fill down to [38] days, and the in-house team kept ownership of every req. The surge model is now part of their annual workforce planning going forward

Hiring spikes are not the problem. Being surprised by them is.

Everyone is building an AI harness right now. Rule files, agent configs, instruction sets, guardrails.

Almost nobody is building the thing the harness depends on.

A harness decides what gets into your codebase. To decide anything, it needs evidence that a change did damage: contracts, tests, signals that fire when something breaks. Without that layer underneath, a harness is a set of rules enforced against nothing.

I think it gets skipped because it doesn't look new. Harnesses feel like the AI-native part. Tests feel like 2015.

I wrote about why that order is backwards, and about what antibiotic resistance has to do with any of it: https://lnkd.in/dF6PpX7J

This is the work I want to be doing, and I'm looking for a team to do it in. Engineering Manager or Engineering Director, at a product company. Vilnius, or remote in the EU.

If you're hiring, or you know a team sitting on this problem, send me a message.

I opened one of my applications last night and looked at the dates instead of the rate.

Submitted 27 August. Interview completed 9 May.

I did not sit an interview for that role. I sat one interview, once, in May. Every application I have made since has reused it.

If you have spent this year job hunting the conventional way, sit with that for a second.

In the market most of us come from, every role is a fresh assessment. New form. New screening call. New competency interview. New panel. Everything you proved to the last employer is worth nothing to the next one, and you begin at zero each time. That is not a minor inefficiency. It is most of what makes a job search exhausting.

Here the assessment happens once and then persists. It sits in a profile and gets read every time a role needs that evidence, whether you are watching or not.

Which changes what you are actually building. You are not running a job search. You are building an asset that gets read repeatedly.

It also changes what a setback costs. Projects on this model end, sometimes early, and that is written into the contract terms on the listing itself. But when a project concludes, your profile does not. The interview stays completed. 

Your other contracts are untouched. In a conventional career, losing a role sends you back to the start of every assessment process in the market. Here, a project ending costs you the project.

Edition 25 is live, with the FP&A Expert role that mechanic just put in front of me. Senior FP&A professionals, $80 to $90 an hour, remote, US GAAP and IFRS tracks.

If you have run a budget cycle and defended a variance to a board, read it.

Someone spent hundreds of millions of dollars teaching a model to think. You
get to teach that same model your job for pocket change.

That's fine-tuning.

Training a model from zero costs a fortune and a data center. Fine-tuning 
skips all of it. You take one that already speaks fluent language and show 
it a few thousand examples from your world, your contracts, your support 
tickets, your house style, until it stops sounding generic and starts sounding like you.
 
Picture the alternative: raising a lawyer from birth just to review one 
contract. Hiring a sharp generalist and teaching them your practice 
area? That's what we're talking about here.
 
It's why hundreds of "custom AI" products exist without anyone training a 
model from scratch. They're standing on a giant's shoulders and adding the 
last mile.

As you might remember: 
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) changes what's in the prompt.  It's like providing some additional files or context before your AI answers.  
 
Fine-tuning changes the models weights...it's like sending an employee to a training course.

Reinforcement learning is like telling the model what "good" or "great" looks like...these are like the performance reviews that we give to AI to shape their habits.

👇 If you could teach an AI one thing about how you work, what would it be?

“You need a degree to get experience.”

No, you don’t.

One of the biggest career traps is believing you need permission before you can start building relevant experience.

Employers say they want experience. So give them evidence that you can do the work.

You can build relevant experience without a degree:

• Freelance. Take small projects—even if they don’t pay much initially. You’re building a track record.

• Volunteer strategically. Help a nonprofit, small business, or community organization solve a real problem related to the career you want.

• Build something. Create a website. Analyze a public dataset. Develop a marketing plan. Write an industry report. Build an app. Create a portfolio.

• Get certified. In many fields, a respected industry certification can demonstrate practical knowledge faster and more cheaply than a four-year degree.

• Learn the tools employers actually use. Software, AI platforms, analytics tools, CRM systems, project-management platforms—whatever appears repeatedly in job descriptions.

• Take contract or entry-level work. Your first job doesn’t need to be your dream job. It needs to give you skills, accomplishments, and references.

• Document your results. “Helped with social media” isn’t compelling. “Increased LinkedIn engagement 42% in three months” is.

The goal isn’t to recreate college without going to college.

The goal is to create evidence of competence.

A degree is a credential.

Experience is proof.

And increasingly, employers aren’t just asking, “Where did you go to school?”

They’re asking the question that matters:

“Show me what you can do.”

71% of workers stay in toxic jobs. Not because they want to. Because they are afraid.

This is the hidden crisis of the modern workforce.

The fear is specific. Financial pressures make leaving feel impossible. Unstable hiring markets offer no safety net. Automation threatens to eliminate entire categories of work . Employees watch colleagues disappear. They read about AI driven layoffs. They understand that relevance is no longer inherited but continuously earned.

Why does this happen?

The workplace has fundamentally restructured itself. Job stability no longer exists. Career paths no longer follow predictable lines. The social contract has been replaced by a transactional arrangement where loyalty receives no reciprocity. Workers have learned that staying is safer than seeking. The devil they know seems preferable to the unknown.

Why will it continue?

FOBO, the fear of becoming obsolete, now grips the workforce . AI systems write emails, analyse data, draft contracts, diagnose illnesses, and generate code . Tasks that once defined careers are being emptied one by one. Workers who resist automation tools isolate themselves further. Workers who embrace them still know that their own expertise may eventually be extracted and replicated.

The result is paralysis. Employees stop volunteering ideas. They delay decisions. They overwork, hoping effort alone will outpace irrelevance . They stay in toxic environments because leaving feels like jumping from one precarious situation into another.

Moody At Work breaks this cycle. Through continuous employee engagement tracking, organizations identify toxic patterns before they drive talent away. Recognition programs reinforce value when fear undermines confidence. Anonymous feedback channels give employees voice without risking retaliation. Leaders receive real time data on team sentiment, enabling proactive intervention rather than reactive damage control. Employees who feel valued stop feeling trapped. Organizations that listen stop losing talent.

I see a lot of recruiters posting about fake candidates and AI, which I understand. From a candidate perspective, if you're approaching one of us about a role, be as specific as you can about your background, who you work for, the company and the job description. If I can't verify who you are, there's much less of a chance I'm going to work with you or have interest in the company. 

If you can't send a job description to an actual company website, that's a big red flag. If you can't mention the pay grade or job location (on site, remote, hybrid, city, etc), that's a big red flag. If you can't tell us whether or not the job is permanent, contract work, or part time, again, big red flag. 

Ideally, the more transparency you can give to us as job seekers, the more comfortable many of us feel about working with you, your company, or your recruiting agency. 

Transparency goes both ways. Job scams are real out there. Don't just give out your personal info from someone pretending to have a job that may fit your background. Do thorough checks on them just as they are doing checks on you. 

Fake jobs and fake recruiters hurt real recruiters and hiring managers hiring for real roles at real companies. I don't understand why this is even legal, but here we are. If you're a recruiter posting fake jobs, shame on you. If you're posing as a recruiter, then also shame on you. 

There are real recruiters, HR professionals, and real companies hiring real people for real jobs out there. In an already difficult labor market, fake jobs makes it that much harder for us to trust them. 

Posting fake jobs should be illegal, end of story or lying to the workforce that you have an intent of hiring someone when there really wasn't. Or pretending to be a recruiter or legitimate company when you're not. 

I don't understand how that's not a form of fraudulent advertising.
